s1.syndrome_frame: Sudden onset of bilateral vision loss following trauma
salient_findings: Normal anterior and posterior segment examinations
No abnormalities on noncontrast computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
key_facts: 30-year-old man with no prior medical or psychiatric history
Sudden onset of painless bilateral loss of vision
Vision loss occurred immediately after a fall from a pickup truck
Patient had a concussion and a superficial scalp laceration
Initial visual acuity was counting fingers bilaterally
Visual acuity decreased to no light perception in both eyes the following day
Systemic and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable
Relative afferent pupillary defect testing, fogging test, and menace reflex were all normal
Noncontrast computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed no abnormalities
Visual evoked potentials were normal
Electroretinography indicated no pathologic process

shortlist.label: Traumatic optic neuropathy
shortlist.why_kept: Sudden onset of bilateral vision loss following trauma

shortlist.label: Conversion disorder
shortlist.why_kept: Inconclusive findings and normal diagnostic tests

shortlist.label: Cortical blindness
shortlist.why_kept: Bilateral vision loss with normal anterior and posterior segment examinations

shortlist.label: Bilateral optic neuropathy
shortlist.why_kept: Painless bilateral vision loss with normal pupillary reflexes

shortlist.label: Postconcussive syndrome
shortlist.why_kept: Vision loss following a concussion with no other clear explanation

raw.rationale: The patient's vision loss occurred immediately after a traumatic event, and the lack of abnormalities on brain imaging and electrophysiological tests suggests a peripheral cause of vision loss, such as traumatic optic neuropathy, which is a subtype of the broader category of optic neuropathies that could be related to the anchor label of Cortical blindness in terms of severe visual impairment but is more specific to the optic nerve damage likely caused by the trauma.

rejected.label: Cortical blindness
rejected.why: Normal visual evoked potentials and lack of brain abnormalities on imaging make cortical blindness less likely

rejected.label: Conversion disorder
rejected.why: The sudden onset of vision loss immediately after a traumatic event and the presence of a plausible organic cause make conversion disorder less likely

rejected.label: Bilateral optic neuropathy
rejected.why: While possible, traumatic optic neuropathy is a more specific diagnosis given the traumatic context

rejected.label: Postconcussive syndrome
rejected.why: Vision loss is not a typical symptom of postconcussive syndrome, and the specific nature of the visual impairment points towards a more direct injury to the optic nerves
